description_full: Sanrio Company, Ltd., together with its subsidiaries, plans and sells social communication gifts, greeting cards, and books in Japan, Europe, North America, South America, rest of Asia, and internationally. It also operates restaurants; and produces, promotes, and distributes movies. In addition, it engages in the planning, production, and sale of recorded music and video products; planning and presentation of musicals and live performances; copyright licensing; planning and operation of theme parks; planning, development, and sale of educational services and materials; planning, sale, and distribution of digital content; planning and sale of merchandise and publications; production and sale of video software; and advertising, marketing, and sports activities. Further, the company engages in the sale and rental of robots, rental of cars, and non-life insurance agency services. Sanrio Company, Ltd. was incorporated in 1949 and is headquartered in Shinagawa, Japan.

financial_summary: Sanrio Company, Ltd. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $8.6B market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +34% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +7.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 86% against a 7% cost of capital — a 78-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 74% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $294M in free cash flow — roughly 24 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.96× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and within its sector the business captures 5.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 40% operating margin runs 33pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 5.05x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 21% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 29% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 70% and a beta of 0.53, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $6K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
val: The stock trades 39% below its DCF fair value of $23.31, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 25%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $15.09 to $37.13 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 24.4 vs 18.8 and P/FCF 29.2 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.4% (below the risk-free rate).
The price implies 10.5% annual cash-flow growth, 9pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 86% clears the cost of capital of 7.4% by 78pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.59).
It runs a 74% gross margin and converts 24% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9.
ROE of 35% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
SG&A jumped 33% last year, worth watching.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $666.4M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 13.8, in the safe zone).
The Beneish M-score (-2.16) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 33.9% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 20% of profits supports about 16.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: It returns 2.2% a year to shareholders (1.1% in buybacks and 1.2% in dividends).
people: With about 2,157 employees, each generates about $563K of revenue, 1.5x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $136K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.2M (2x revenue per employee).
